content: 1. Townsend et al. (2012) evaluated the effectiveness of respondent-driven sampling (RDS) in recruiting high-risk heterosexual men with multiple female sexual partners. They analyzed differences in HIV prevalence and sexual risk behaviors at two distinct time points. Their findings were published in AIDS Behavior. 2. Townsend et al. (2013) estimated HIV prevalence and associated risk behaviors among heterosexual women with multiple sexual partners in a high-risk South African community using RDS. This study was detailed in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 3. Heckathorn (2007) expanded on RDS methodology by addressing the analysis of continuous variables and controlling for differential recruitment. This work was published in Sociological Methodology. 4. Goel and Salganik (2010) assessed the reliability of RDS as a sampling method, with their findings published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA. 5. Gile and Handcock (2010) critically evaluated the current methodologies of RDS in Sociological Methodology, highlighting its strengths and limitations. 6. Gile (2011) proposed improved inference techniques for RDS data, particularly for estimating HIV prevalence. This research appeared in the Journal of the American Statistical Association. 7. Volz and Heckathorn (2008) developed a probability-based estimation theory for RDS, which was published in the Journal of Official Statistics. 8. Gile, Johnston, and Salganik (2015) introduced diagnostic tools for RDS studies, which were discussed in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. 9. Wejnert and Heckathorn (2008) explored the efficiency and efficacy of web-based RDS for online research, with their findings published in Sociological Methods and Research. 10. Johnston et al. (2008) documented the challenges of implementing RDS for HIV biological and behavioral surveillance in international settings. Their experiences were shared in AIDS Behavior. 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean developed a guide for using RDS Analyst and NetDraw for HIV/AIDS and sexually transmitted infection surveillance. This guide was published as Module 4 of their surveillance series. 12. Heckathorn (2002) introduced RDS II, a methodology for deriving valid population estimates from chain-referral samples of hidden populations. This work was published in Social Problems. 13. Semaan et al. (2010) discussed the ethical considerations of surveys employing RDS in the American Journal of Public Health. 14. White et al. (2015) proposed the STROBE-RDS statement to improve the reporting of observational studies using RDS. This was published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 15. The WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean also published an introduction to RDS as part of their HIV/AIDS surveillance guidelines. 16. Global Health Sciences developed a toolbox for conducting integrated HIV bio-behavioral surveillance (IBBS) in key populations, accessible through their website. 17. Sample size requirements for surveys are influenced by statistical and resource considerations. Factors such as sampling speed, duration, and implementation challenges can affect the actual sample size achieved. 18. Sample size calculations for probability-based surveys should consider confidence intervals, design effects, and precision. Consulting a statistician is recommended for complex survey designs. 19. Design effects quantify how much larger a sample size must be for complex survey designs compared to simple random sampling. This accounts for increased variance in non-random sampling methods. 20. Missing data, non-responses, and specimen loss can impact survey results. To mitigate this, an increase in sample size is recommended during survey planning. 21. Finite population corrections should be applied when the sample size is not significantly smaller than the population size. 22. Calculating sample size to detect changes over time involves determining the initial prevalence, the size of the difference to be detected, significance levels, and statistical power. Larger differences require smaller sample sizes to detect statistically significant changes. 23. Statistical power reflects the likelihood of detecting a true change in proportions over time. Typically, 80% power is selected, meaning there is an 80% chance of detecting a change if it exists. 24. 25. Population size estimation is critical for understanding the scope of HIV epidemics, planning programs, and monitoring their effectiveness. Multiple estimation methods should be used to derive consensus estimates. 26. The UNAIDS program uses population size estimates to calculate the number of new and prevalent infections, individuals eligible for care, and HIV-related deaths. These estimates also guide funding and program planning. 27. Population size estimation methods vary, and no single gold standard exists. Combining multiple methods can provide more reliable estimates. This text provides a detailed and professional summary of the referenced studies and methodologies, emphasizing their relevance to HIV research and surveillance.
